title: Merge K Sorted Lists
description: Pairwise divide-and-conquer: merge lists in pairs, then pairs of pairs, until one remains. Each level merges N total nodes; log k levels gives O(N log k).

notes: Pairwise merge beats naive merge-into-accumulator: that approach is O(N*k), this one is O(N log k).
Use a dummy head in mergeTwo so you never special-case the first append.
Attach the trailing tail with `tail.next = a || b` — the surviving list is already sorted.
A min-heap of (val, listIndex) also achieves O(N log k); pairwise merge avoids importing a heap.

questions.q: Why is pairwise merge O(N log k) but merging one-list-at-a-time is O(N*k)?
options: Pairwise has fewer comparisons per merge
Each node is rewritten O(log k) times instead of O(k) times

questions.q: What does the dummy head in mergeTwo buy you?
options: Avoids a special case for the first node — tail.next always means the same thing

questions.q: After the inner while exits with one list null, what do you do with the survivor?
options: Attach via tail.next = a || b — it is already sorted

questions.q: Time complexity for k sorted lists with N nodes total?

exercises.prompt: Fill in pairwise merge. mergeTwo uses a dummy + tail; mergeKLists halves the list count each round.

blanks.hint: advance tail to the node you just attached
whichever list still has nodes — attach its remainder
keep merging until exactly one list remains

L3.prompt: Write `mergeKLists(lists)` using pairwise divide-and-conquer with a `mergeTwo` helper. Use the toList/toArr helpers. Log `JSON.stringify(toArr(mergeKLists([toList([1,4,5]), toList([1,3,4]), toList([2,6])])))`.
hints: Write mergeTwo first with a dummy + tail; rewire pointers in place.
In mergeKLists, loop while lists.length > 1, pairing consecutive lists each round.
Odd-length round: the last unpaired list merges with null — mergeTwo handles that.
